did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a clear declaration of faith: God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart, even though the rest of the psalm describes a crisis and doubt.
Did you know? The psalmist honestly admits that he nearly went astray: he describes his condition as though his feet had almost slipped and his steps had nearly given way.
Did you know? The source of the psalmist’s envy is not wealth alone, but especially the apparent ease of the wicked and their success in the world.
Did you know? According to the psalm’s description, the wicked’s pride is not merely an inner feeling: it becomes their necklace and clothing, while violence covers them.
Did you know? The speech of the wicked is portrayed as having cosmic ambition: their mouths seem to reach the heavens, and their tongues roam the earth, influencing everything.
Did you know? The psalmist raises the difficult question of whether keeping his heart pure and washing his hands was in vain, since the righteous person still faces affliction and suffering.
Did you know? The turning point in the psalm comes when the psalmist enters the sanctuary of God; there he understands the fate of the wicked, after being unable to understand it on his own.
Did you know? The fate of the wicked is compared to a dream that disappears upon waking—a picture emphasizing its fleeting nature and the gap between apparent prosperity and its end.
Did you know? After confessing his ignorance, the psalmist describes his relationship with God as God holding him by the right hand—a picture of presence, support, and guidance.
Did you know? The psalm’s conclusion is that being near God is the true good: the psalmist chooses God as his refuge and commits to telling of all his works.
